name: Trill-Fragment
geological_features: Irregular shape suggesting a fragment of a larger body
Exposed crystalline interior on one face
Micro-crater peppering on the space-facing surface
specific_features: The Trill Face — an exposed crystal face that vibrates at high frequency when struck by solar wind, producing detectable radio oscillations
A flat, smooth fracture surface where the fragment separated from its parent body
resources: Iron-nickel alloy at the exposed core face
description: Trill-Fragment is barely a world at all — an irregular chunk of rock and crystal less than a thousand kilometers across, clearly a fragment of a much larger body that was destroyed or disrupted long ago. Its most remarkable feature is the Trill Face, a large exposed surface of piezoelectric crystal that vibrates when struck by solar wind particles, producing a rapid oscillation detectable as radio emissions.

The fragment tumbles slowly through space, rotating on two axes simultaneously and presenting different faces to the sun in an irregular pattern. The Trill Face emissions fluctuate accordingly, producing a complex, warbling radio signature that was initially mistaken for an artificial signal. The fragment's gravity is negligible — landing on it is more like docking with a spacecraft than touching down on a planet.

Analysis of the fracture surfaces and composition suggests the fragment was once part of a terrestrial-class planet that was destroyed by a massive impact approximately two billion years ago. The crystalline interior was likely deep within the parent body, protected from space exposure until the destruction event. Other fragments from the same body have been identified in the surrounding space, but none share the piezoelectric properties of the Trill Face.

The Trill Face crystal is of significant scientific and commercial interest. Its natural piezoelectric properties are superior to any synthetic equivalent, and samples have been used to develop ultra-sensitive detection equipment. However, the crystal cannot be removed without destroying the radio emissions that make the fragment scientifically interesting. A compromise allows small samples to be taken from the edges while preserving the active central surface, but the crystal is finite and the demand growing.
